newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia to deepen ties with Western groups at G7.
newsitem.headline: Russia to deepen ties with Western groups at G7.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin will celebrate a personal triumph when he takes his seat at a summit with seven industrial democracies this week and deepens Russia's integration with global economic organisations.

The 66-year-old Kremlin leader missed last year's Group of Seven summit to fight off a communist election challenge. Now recovered from heart surgery and pneumonia, he goes to this year's meeting in Denver stronger politically and physically than 12 months ago.

Russia is not a G7 member. But Yeltsin emerged from tough talks this year on NATO's eastward expansion, which Moscow had been resisting fiercely, with the bonus of an enhanced role to play at this year's three-day summit starting on Friday.
"Russia sees it as a question of prestige, and its motives when it comes to joining the G7 are mainly political," said Alexander Bykov, an independent Russian economic analyst.
"It is a question of being a great country, and sitting at the same table as other great countries to discuss all issues."

Yeltsin, who has taken part in political discussions at four previous G7 summits, will also now join in talks on selected economic matters, such as how to cope with ageing populations and how to design social safety nets to serve them.
He will be excluded from only one session, an hour-long discussion on economic and financial issues.

Yeltsin is sure to press Moscow's case for joining the G7 and turning it into the G8. This would recognise the progress of Russia's reforms since the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991 and enhance its status as a political and economic, as well as nuclear, power.

"What is the Russian Federation's main goal as it approaches the summit? Above all it is hoping for new steps in the full formation of the G8, and increasing the status of Russia in this mechanism," said Vadim Lukov, head of the Russian foreign ministry's international policy department.
He said Moscow would also want to discuss its admission to the World Trade Organisation, the Paris Club of creditor nations and the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development.

Russia is unlikely to join the G7 yet. It has a much weaker economy than those of the seven members -- the United States, Japan, France, Germany, Britain, Italy and Canada -- and the transition from a communist economy is proving difficult.
But U.S. officials say Russia's bigger role is justified by its weight in the world and is in the G7 countries' interest.
They say Moscow's cooperation is vital on issues such as international crime-fighting and promoting nuclear safety, and are calling the Denver meeting the "Summit of the Eight".
The G7 leaders still regard Yeltsin as a guarantor of reforms in Russia and realise that an expanded role at the G7 could boost Moscow's appeal to potential investors.
President Bill Clinton, anxious to support Yeltsin, promised to promote Moscow's integration with the international economic community at a U.S.-Russian summit in Helsinki last March.

That helped compensate Russia for NATO's planned expansion into former communist eastern Europe. A new partnership deal with NATO, and Russia's new role in the G7, have helped Yeltsin to claim foreign policy successes in recent months, despite criticism from his opponents.

"It is part of the West's psychotherapy for Russia, and for Yeltsin personally, to let him say that Russia is very important," said Andrei Piontkovsky, head of Moscow's indpendent Centre for Strategic Studies.
Yeltsin will also hold talks with Clinton, Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on the fringes of the summit.
